newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Allianz says it has no Creditanstalt ambitions.
newsitem.headline: Allianz says it has no Creditanstalt ambitions.

text.p: Germany's Allianz on Tuesday said it was not interested in Austrian privatisation candidate Creditanstalt, countering speculation in Austria media the insurance giant may re-enter the six-year long sell-off race.

"We are interested in acquiring a sales network for our products at bank counters, and this is true in Austria as well," Allianz spokesman Lothar Landgraf told Reuters. "But we are not interested in acquiring Creditanstalt."

Allianz Holding last year teamed up with Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank to bid for the Austrian government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt, but soon dropped its offer in anger over a due diligence process it felt was biased against foreigners.

Daily Der Standard on Tuesday reported Allianz had once again cast an eye on Creditanstalt, but that it was holding off with a new offer until the government had officially declared the chase open again.

Rumours started flying this weekend when Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima said he was unhappy with a lone last-minute bid by a consortium around Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali and hinted he may reopen the chase, already Austria's longest-running privatisation project, to other potential buyers.

The group, which includes Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana, on Friday made an offer for Creditanstalt hours before a midnight deadline expired, but Klima said the proposal was too vague.

Klima, who has enlisted JP Morgan as his advisors in the sale of the country's second-largest bank, is expected to brief the weekly cabinet meeting about the affair later on Tuesday. A final decision could take up to two weeks, he has indicated.

Italian-controlled EA-Generali said its proposal was an "updated version" of a bid the group made last October, when it offered to pay nine billion schillings ($851.5 million) for about two thirds of the government's Creditanstalt stake and sell the remainder in a secondary offering.

Only sketchy details of the offer have been leaked, but sources close to the negotiations said the new bid is not for all of the government's 19.9 million ordinary shares in the flagship bank. The government has repeatedly said it wants an all-cash offer for its entire Creditanstalt stake.

A rejection of that bid may give a much-needed boost to Die Erste's hitherto unsuccesful attempts to get its hands on Austria's best-known finance house and one-time banker to the Austro-Hungarian empire.

Die Erste, the country's leading savings bank, on Friday split with the consortium around EA-Generali, disillusioned over its erstwhile partners' refusal to accept its proposal for a joint holding with Creditanstalt under Die Erste's control.
The scorned savings bank on Monday said it was still interested in playing a role in the privatisation and indicated it was now on the lookout for new partners.
"You'll always find a partner if you're beautiful and rich," an Erste spokesman told Austrian news agency APA. "We are beautiful and rich."

Die Erste is barely a third the size of Creditanstalt, which has total assets of almost 700 billion schillings and has over the past years become one of the most successful players on the emerging markets of eastern and central Europe. ($1=10.57 Schilling)
